title: The Economic Impacts of Climate Change: Evidence from Agricultural Output and Random Fluctuations in Weather
research_question: What is the effect of long-run changes in temperature and precipitation on the profitability and productivity of the U.S. agricultural sector, and how are these economic impacts distributed across regions and crops?
data_description: The analysis uses a county-level panel constructed from the 1978, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002 Censuses of Agriculture, covering a balanced sample of roughly 2,268 U.S. counties (excluding Alaska and Hawaii). Key outcomes include agricultural profits per acre (revenues minus production expenses), the value of land and buildings per acre, and crop yields (bushels per acre planted) for corn for grain and soybeans. Soil quality measures (K-factor, slope length, flood-proneness, sand/clay content, irrigation share, permeability, salinity, etc.) come from the National Resource Inventory. Weather data are derived from PRISM (4km grid monthly precipitation/temperature) and NCDC daily station data, used to construct growing-season degree-days (base 46.4°F, ceiling 89.6°F) and total growing-season precipitation. Climate change projections come from the IPCC benchmark scenario (uniform +5°F, +8% precipitation) and the Hadley 2 model for medium-term (2020–2049) and long-term (2070–2099) horizons.
institutional_context: Agricultural production depends directly on temperature and precipitation, making farming one of the sectors most exposed to anthropogenic climate change. Projected increases in greenhouse gas concentrations are expected to raise U.S. growing-season temperatures by several degrees and modestly increase precipitation by the end of the twenty-first century, with substantial heterogeneity across states and between irrigated and non-irrigated regions. Farmers can adjust input use (fertilizer, irrigation water) within a season and, over longer horizons, switch crops or convert land to non-agricultural uses. The U.S. agricultural sector is also shaped by federal commodity programs, land markets that capitalize expected future rents into farmland values, and regional differences in soil quality, urbanization pressure, and access to irrigation. Prior estimates of climate damages to U.S. agriculture have been highly inconclusive, motivating a setting in which year-to-year weather realizations within counties can be exploited to learn about climate impacts.
